title: Repositioning PostHog
summary: As PostHog enters its next chapter , we have spent the last 6 weeks going all in repositioning as the company that makes your product self-driving…
body_text: Repositioning PostHog Charles Cook Jul 23, 2026 PostHog news , Inside PostHog Contents As PostHog enters its next chapter , we have spent the last 6 weeks going all in repositioning as the company that makes your product self-driving. This is how we are specifically doing it, and how it's going. If you are trying to position or reposition your product, hopefully this will help you! What does repositioning actually mean? "Positioning" is when you set the context for how you want your product to be seen by customers. You're trying to get across how your product is the best in the world at something that your ideal customer profile (ICP) actually cares about. "Repositioning" is when you change your positioning (woah). It's very normal to regularly review your positioning as the world around you changes. Why did PostHog need repositioning? We originally positioned PostHog as open source product analytics for developers back in 2020. Over time, we've expanded to position ourselves as a suite of tools that product engineers use to build better products. We've used terms like "Product OS" and "customer data infrastructure" that tried to capture this. Despite this, most people still see PostHog as "analytics++" today even though we make money from a lot of different products. In part, this was because we did our repositioning incrementally, but mostly it's because repositioning is just hard , especially if you don't go all in. We updated website copy! We ran ads! We wrote blogs! But never all at once, and never in a way that felt like our entire team was pointing in the same direction and moving with the same urgency. How PostHog is positioned now Self-driving is now how we are positioning ourselves. We are going all in on this in an uncomfortable way - this means putting it front and center on our website, but also focusing on it in content , video , influencers , events etc. Being all in means realizing this will probably confuse some people for a bit. It might hurt signups. We are willing to tolerate some short term pain, because we believe our long term success (and revenue!) depends on convincing people that you build with PostHog, not add it on afterwards. I feel like we wouldn't have a shot at doing this well if it weren't for the fact that our founders are totally bought in on this - it has to come top down. You can see more in our public handbook , but here's the tl;dr: PostHog makes your product self-driving. Products are the surfaces a customer adopts to access self-driving. Today that's PostHog Web , PostHog Slack , PostHog MCP , PostHog CLI , and PostHog Desktop . PostHog Mobile is coming. Tools are the capabilities you access through the products: product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, surveys, web analytics, and so on. Tools can be as granular as annotations or comments even. Context is the data that feeds the self-driving loop: events, recordings, errors, and logs from PostHog, plus other business data (Slack, code, Notion, support tickets etc.) Context warehouse is the managed data warehouse plus the full context-ingestion pipeline (modelling, data pipelines, batch exports, and so on). A large part of positioning comes down to some sets of specific words you are going to repeat everywhere until you are bored of them. They need to be specific and limited because our audience's attention is limited. Once your team is bored of hearing them from you, chances are that your customers have only just started to internalize them. Where is PostHog playing now if not analytics? We're now positioning ourselves as part of the market for self-driving software product platforms. We don't have a perfect competitor in terms of overlap, but some are reasonably close if you squint, especially if they are shipping "self-healing" or "self-improving" software. The truest competitor for our ICP that we should care about is the old way of working. Triaging errors, watching replays back, writing the PR yourself, re-prompting an agent for every change, connecting your warehouse to your analytics to your coding tool - these are the habits that we are offering an alternative to. Why are you inventing new concepts like self-driving and context warehouse? When you're playing in a fuzzily defined or emerging market, you enter the realm of category creation. This is different to most positioning, where you are in an established market differentiating yourself against existing companies and products. Category creation is fun, high risk, and hard to pull off. Rather than building "Uber for dogs", you are trying to change people's mental model for how an established thing should work. This sometimes requires you to come up with new terms to describe what're you are doing, because it doesn't exist yet. When a term has been widely adopted in the industry, we will use that term - we would not try and redefine "MCP" as something else for example. However, "self-driving" and "context warehouse" describe things that don't really exist today, or where there isn't consensus yet. You may have heard the concept of "self-healing" or "self-improving" software for example, but these are very far from industry standards. We have to work really hard to educate people about these new terms, to the point of feeling like we're repeating ourselves too much. We're confident we can succeed because we have some prior experience helping to popularize the concept of "product engineer". We didn't invent the term, but were one of the earliest people to hire product engineers, wrote about it a bunch (top of Google when you search the term), and now it feels pretty standard. Are you open to changing your minds about this? Maybe one day! But not right now - internally, we've had plenty of rounds of feedback and we've all had to disagree and commit to some extent to get this out there. Debating product names is the perfect way to distract your entire team for hours. Part of repositioning is that you really have to commit to it for several months to see if it's landing. And of course, we'll change course if things look like they're going wrong. Early signs are promising from some of our best customers, and people are starting to talk about it on places like X. But it's only been a few weeks, and the majority of mentions still talk about us in the context of analytics -we'll get there. As has always been the case, we will know whether we need to change course by talking to our users and making something they want . This was mildly useful, but I'd appreciate a book recommendation There are a million books about positioning. They are all compromised in some way. I speed ran April Dunford's process in a week from Obviously Awesome , and it's worked well enough for us. PostHog is the leading platform for building self-driving products. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability , product analytics , session replay , feature flags , experiments , error tracking , logs , and more – PostHog captures all the context agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack , the web app , the desktop ( PostHog Desktop ), or your own editor via the MCP . Community questions

title: How to Make Money on X in 2026: 7 Proven Strategies That Work

body_text: Make money on X — that’s what Tobi typed into her notes app at 1 a.m., right after watching a thread from a small creator who claimed to have made $3,200 from a single viral post. Tobi had over 4,000 followers on X, a decent engagement rate, and absolutely no idea how any of it translated into actual cash. She reposted hot takes, argued about Afrobeats rankings, and dropped the occasional career tip. Yet nothing she did ever showed up as income. So she did what most curious Nigerians do: she started digging. What Tobi found surprised her. People weren’t getting rich from luck or follower count. They were treating X like a business channel, not just a timeline to scroll through. Once she understood the systems behind it, she stopped guessing and started building. Within four months, Tobi had turned her account into a small but steady income stream — and she’s not alone. Thousands of creators, freelancers, and side hustlers across Nigeria are learning to make money on X in 2026, and you can join them too. This guide breaks down exactly how to make money on X in 2026, using strategies that actually work whether you’re starting from zero or already have an audience. What Does It Mean to Make Money on X? To make money on X simply means turning your posts, presence, and audience into income, either directly through the platform or indirectly through opportunities it creates. Direct monetisation includes features built into X itself, such as ad revenue sharing, subscriptions, and tips. Indirect monetisation happens when your content on X leads to clients, brand deals, or sales elsewhere. Most people who successfully make money on X don’t rely on a single method. Instead, they stack two or three strategies together so one slow week doesn’t wipe out their entire income. That’s exactly the mindset this guide encourages. How Much Can You Make on X in 2026? Earnings vary widely, but there’s a rough pattern. Beginners who are learning to make money on X usually earn between $50 and $300 a month once they find early traction. Intermediate creators with an engaged following often make money on X in the $300 to $2,000 range monthly. Advanced creators who combine several income streams can make money on X well beyond $5,000 a month. None of this happens overnight, so treat the first 90 days as groundwork rather than payday. 7 Proven Ways to Make Money on X in 2026 1. Join X’s Creator Revenue Sharing Program One of the most direct ways to make money on X is through its Creator Revenue Sharing program. This feature pays you a share of advertising revenue based on engagement from Premium subscribers. Consequently, the more meaningful replies and interactions your posts attract, the more you stand to earn. To qualify, you typically need an active Premium subscription, at least 500 Premium followers, and roughly 5 million impressions over three months. These numbers sound intimidating at first, but consistent, conversation-starting content gets you there faster than viral luck ever will. 2. Offer Paid Subscriptions Subscriptions let you make money on X by giving your most loyal followers access to exclusive content for a monthly fee. Instead of posting everything publicly, you can reserve deeper insights, behind-the-scenes updates, or niche resources for paying subscribers. Because this model rewards consistency rather than virality, even a modest, engaged audience can generate real income. For instance, 150 subscribers paying $5 monthly adds up to $750 every single month, without a single viral post required. 3. Collect Tips From Your Audience Tips offer one of the simplest ways to make money on X because they don’t depend on algorithms, thresholds, or follower counts. Once you link a supported payment method, your audience can send you money directly whenever your content resonates with them. Tips usually start small. However, as your community grows more loyal, so does their willingness to support you financially, especially when you make the ask feel natural rather than desperate. 4. Promote Products Through Affiliate Marketing Affiliate marketing is an accessible way to make money on X since you don’t need to build your own product first. Instead, you share a referral link and earn a commission whenever someone buys through it. The creators who succeed here avoid pushy sales posts. Rather, they weave recommendations into tutorials, honest reviews, or personal experiences, which builds trust and, in turn, drives more conversions. 5. Sell Your Own Digital Products or Services If you want to make money on X with the highest ceiling, selling your own products or services is the way to go. This could mean ebooks, templates, online courses, or consulting packages that you fully own and control. Because you keep most of the revenue yourself, this method scales far better than affiliate commissions over time. Your X account simply becomes the storefront that showcases your expertise and builds the trust needed to convert followers into paying customers. 6. Land Sponsored Posts and Brand Deals As your following grows, you can also make money on X through sponsored content, where brands pay you to promote their products directly to your audience. Importantly, you don’t need a massive following to start; a smaller, highly engaged audience in a specific niche often performs better than a large, passive one. Brands increasingly favour authenticity over sheer numbers. So, if you consistently post valuable, niche-specific content, expect pitches to come in as your engagement climbs. 7. Use X to Attract Freelance Clients Finally, freelancers can make money on X without waiting on any platform feature at all. Rather than depending solely on job boards, you can use your posts as a live portfolio that showcases your thinking, your process, and your results. Over time, this consistent visibility attracts clients who already trust you before they ever send a message. As a result, you spend less time on cold pitches and more time delivering paid work. How to Withdraw and Receive Your X Earnings in Nigeria Learning how to make money on X is only half the equation; receiving that money without losing a chunk of it to fees or delays is the other half. X processes creator payouts through Stripe, which means your earnings typically land in a Stripe-connected account before you can withdraw them. From there, Nigerian creators often hit a wall: local banks aren’t always built for international payouts, and conversion rates can quietly eat into your income. This is exactly where Cleva changes the equation. With a Cleva USD account, you can receive your X earnings in dollars, hold them safely, and convert to naira only when the rate works in your favour. Cleva also offers a virtual dollar card, the Cleva Classic Card, which lets you pay for X Premium subscriptions without the usual failed-transaction headaches many Nigerian cardholders face. So whether you’re unlocking Creator Revenue Sharing eligibility or simply paying for tools that help you grow, your card just works. Beyond receiving payouts, Cleva rewards you further.
